summary: Specifies how DNS software should handle resource record types it does not understand, so that new types no longer need changes to name server software. It is a proposed standard.

plainLanguage.summary: DNS can gain new kinds of records, but older servers may not understand them. RFC 3597 tells those servers to preserve and pass on the unfamiliar data so new record types can travel through the DNS.

subtitle: How DNS software can pass along record types it does not recognize.

tldr.problem: Adding a DNS resource record type used to require software changes on authoritative servers, clients, and sometimes intermediate servers.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC requires DNS software to preserve unknown record data as binary, prohibits compression in new types, and defines a generic text representation.
tldr.outcome: New record types can pass through systems that do not understand their data format. RFC 3597 is a Proposed Standard updated by later RFCs.

facts.label: Unknown class notation

facts.value: MUST NOT be allowed for embedded domain names

today: RFC 3597 is a Proposed Standard. It has been updated by RFC 4033, RFC 4034, RFC 4035, RFC 5395, RFC 6195, and RFC 6895.

sections.title: Why Unknown Record Types Matter
sections.content:
The Domain Name System (DNS) can be extended with new resource record (RR) types. Before RFC 3597, deploying one could require software changes not only at the server and client using the type, but also at slave servers and sometimes caches or forwarders.

Changing all those systems is slow and costly. This RFC changes how DNS software handles record types it does not know, allowing new types to pass through without requiring every intermediate server to understand their format.
sections.plainLanguage: DNS needs to support new kinds of records over time. A server that does not know a new kind can still pass it along if it leaves the record data unchanged.

sections.title: What Counts as an Unknown Type
sections.content:
An RR is of unknown type when the DNS implementation does not know its RDATA format, and the type is not an assigned query or meta-type in the ranges described by RFC 2929. If the format depends on the record class, the type and class combination must be unknown for the record to count as unknown.

Name servers and resolvers MUST handle unknown records transparently. They treat RDATA as unstructured binary data and store and transmit it without change. They must also preserve known record data exactly, except where the RFC allows compression or decompression changes, so systems that know and do not know a type can agree on its contents.
sections.plainLanguage: A record is unknown when the server does not know how its data is structured. The server must keep that data exactly as it received it and pass it on unchanged.

sections.title: Why New Types Cannot Use Name Compression
sections.content:
DNS can shorten domain names with compression pointers. A pointer is meaningful only within the DNS message where it appears. Copying a pointer inside record data into a different message could make it point to unrelated bytes and corrupt the name.

Servers MUST NOT compress domain names inside RDATA for class-specific or not-well-known types. The RFC defines only types specified by RFC 1035 as well-known. Future RR specifications that include domain names in RDATA MUST NOT permit compression for those names.

Servers must decompress names in well-known types. The RFC also recommends decompression for several named older types whose specifications have differed on compression. An RR's owner name remains eligible for compression.
sections.plainLanguage: A compression pointer only works in the DNS message that contains it. New record types cannot use compressed names in their data, because copying the pointer into another message could change what it points to.

sections.title: Writing Unknown Records in a Master File
sections.content:
In a master file, an unknown RR type is written as TYPE immediately followed by its decimal type number. An unknown class is written as CLASS followed immediately by its decimal class number. This makes the fields distinguishable from each other and from time-to-live values.

The generic RDATA form begins with \#, followed by the data length in octets as an unsigned decimal integer, followed by zero or more hexadecimal words with an even number of digits. Zero-length data is written as \# 0.

The generic notation may also represent known types, which can make a master file portable. In that case, the server still applies the known type's processing rules.
sections.plainLanguage: A zone file can describe unfamiliar record data with a type number, a byte length, and hexadecimal digits. This lets software store the record without knowing what the data means.

sections.title: Comparisons, DNSSEC, and Additional Processing
sections.content:
Two records of the same unknown type are equal when their RDATA is bit-for-bit equal. Specifications for new types MUST NOT define different comparison rules. As a result, domain names inside unknown data are compared with their letter case preserved.

DNSSEC canonical form lowercases embedded domain names only when the server knows where those names are. RFC 3597 keeps the established canonical form for types first published before this RFC. For other types, embedded names are not lowercased; the owner name is always lowercased.

Unknown types cause no additional section processing. Future type specifications may define such processing, but it must be optional because servers that do not know the type cannot perform it.
sections.plainLanguage: For an unknown record, servers compare the data exactly, including letter case. The RFC also sets consistent DNSSEC rules for embedded names and says unknown records trigger no extra processing.

sections.title: Security and IANA Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC says it is not believed to create new security problems or solve existing ones. Its rules for preserving record data and DNSSEC canonical form help keep processing consistent between servers with different levels of knowledge about a type.

The document requires no IANA actions. Its main change is a handling rule: servers can preserve and pass unknown record data without interpreting it.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC says its changes do not add or remove security protections. IANA has no actions to take.
